extracted.intended_audience: poets, writers, critics, and educated readers interested in composing or judging epigrams, epitaphs, and literary praise
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on composing short, pointed epitaphs and epigrams (and on giving literary praise): how to match tone, be specific and truthful, use irony, and balance panegyric with justice. Also includes wider criteria for what merits praise (industry, genius, application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitaphs as short, pointed praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Epitaphs are 'a sort of Writing which is wholly set apart for a short pointed Method of Praise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep epitaphs concise and pointed; the form calls for brevity and a sharp, focused compliment rather than long exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base praise on real foundation (avoid loose qualifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: When they would praise, they cautiously avoid every looser Qualification, and fix only where there is a real Foundation in Merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ascribe attributes without evidence; praise should rest on demonstrable qualities of the subject rather than vague or extravagant claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid praise that depends on fable
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Praise is trifling when it depends upon Fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If praise relies on myths or doubtful stories, it becomes trifling; ground compliments in believable or actual facts about the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid general, inapplicable praise
rubrics_metrics.description: The Thought here is fine, but its Fault is, that it is general, that it may belong to any great Man... He who gives his Praise in gross, will often appear either to have been a Stranger to those he writes upon, or not to have found any thing in them which is Praise-worthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use broad, generic panegyrics. Specificity shows acquaintance with the subject; general praise often suggests ignorance or laziness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumscribe praise to particular qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be better, if when we light upon such a Turn, we join it with something that circumscribes and bounds it to the Qualities of our Subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pair a general laudatory turn with concrete particulars that anchor the compliment to the individual's real traits or achievements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match tone and humour to the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The Humour is easy and gay, resembling Anacreon in its Air, raised by such Images, and pointed with such a Turn as he might have used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt the style and mood of your praise to fit the subject—e.g., a light, gay tone suits an easy, convivial poet; stylistic consonance strengthens the compliment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of irony as a form of panegyric
rubrics_metrics.description: An Irony is look'd upon as the finest Palliative of Praise; and very often conveys the noblest Panegyrick under the Appearance of Satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony can be an effective vehicle for high praise when it frames a compliment as mock-accusation or playful censure; use carefully so the intent is clear as laudatory, not merely satirical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for a surprising or clever turn
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet slides by, and raises the whole World for a kind of Arbiter, which is to end the Contention amongst its several Parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good epigram or line of praise often includes a witty or unexpected turn that elevates the compliment—skillful surprise increases impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include revealing biographical or civic detail when fitting
rubrics_metrics.description: This Epigram has a respect to the Character of its Subject; for Menander writ remarkably with a Justness and Purity of Language. It has also told the Country he was born in... while it twists together the Glory of the Poet and his Nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate, unobtrusive inclusion of birthplace, civic ties, or characteristic facts can enrich praise and tie the subject to a larger context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evocative imagery strengthens praise
rubrics_metrics.description: I fancied the Poet aimed at the Picture which is generally made of Apollo and the Muses... This look'd beautiful to my Thought, and because the Image arose before me out of the Words of the Original as I was reading it, I venture to explain them so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vivid images (mythic or visual) that resonate with the subject's work can deepen the effect of an epitaph or epigram; be prepared to explicate subtle images for readers if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance lofty praise with justice
rubrics_metrics.description: It is extreamly difficult to hit when we propose to raise Characters high, while we keep to them justly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High commendation should not distort truth; strive to praise generously but fairly, avoiding hyperbole that undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and audience-sensitivity in address
rubrics_metrics.description: You never begin to talk, but when People are desirous to hear you; and I defy any one to be out of humour till you leave off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good speaking or writing gauges the audience and chooses the right moment and length—start when listeners/readers are receptive and stop before weariness sets in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decent, proper language for public contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: They should let their Clients have a little decent and proper English for their Money... that they would leave off such low and unnatural Expressions... What Man that has a Value for a good Name would like to have it said in a publick Court, that Mr. such-a-one was 'stripp'd, saddled' or 'hung up'?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In public or formal forums (e.g., courts), avoid cant, low or coarse expressions and prefer dignified, proper English suited to the occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit-worthy qualities that justify praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Men of the greatest Application and Acquirements... Sir Francis Bacon... Boyle... Leonardo da Vinci—application, study, invention, breadth of attainments, skill in multiple arts, moral qualities agreeable to intellectual endowments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding whom or what to praise, value sustained industry, original contributions, breadth and depth of learning, technical mastery, and moral character; these are proper foundations for lasting fame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivation matters: polish latent talent
rubrics_metrics.description: The Soul is a kind of rough Diamond, which requires Art, Labour, and Time to polish it. For want of which, many a good natural Genius is lost, or lies unfashioned, like a Jewel in the Mine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both natural genius and its cultivation; praise should often recognize the work of education, practice, and refinement as much as innate ability.
